pointer.title: Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Wang Wenbin’s Regular Press Conference on June 14, 2022

record_examples.scope: Exact statement from the published sample viewer

record.text:
Mr. De Rivière (France) (spoke in French): At the outset, I would like to commend the Niger for its unswerving commitment to the fight against climate change and for organizing this debate. This debate provides another opportunity to emphasize that this is environmental fight is also a fight for international peace and security. That is why it is appropriate for the Security Council to address the threats linked to climate change. I welcome the Secretary-General to today’s meeting and thank Mr. Faki Mahamat and Mr. Nuhu for their briefings. Because our world is facing a climate emergency, it is also in permanent danger and is exposed to increased security risks and new threats. The links between climate and security have been firmly established for a long time. We can confirm that everywhere — in the Horn of Africa, in the Sahel and in the Middle East. Desertification, reduced access to water and broader issues related to access to natural resources in rural areas, food shortages and climate insecurity are all factors that allow armed extremist groups to grow by exploiting people’s frustration. We know that in the Sahel terrorist groups exploit inter-ethnic and community conflicts, as well as economic conflicts between farmers and herders, in a context where climate change has significantly changed agropastoral systems. We must do all we can to prevent terrorist groups from taking advantage of the distress caused by the effects of climate change, land degradation and the loss of biodiversity in areas already marked by tensions and fragility. That obviously requires better allocation of natural resources. That is an absolute necessity because

we must not leave the field open for terrorist groups to exploit these conflicts. Furthermore, where there are serious security threats, we must build a virtuous circle between sustainable development and action to preserve the climate. That is the purpose of the Great Green Wall project in the Sahel, a flagship programme to combat the effects of climate change, desertification, food insecurity and poverty from Senegal to Djibouti. The sum of $19 billion has been earmarked for the project, which should make it possible to restore 250 million hectares of degraded land by 2030, create 10 million jobs and capture 250 million tons of carbon. We must also assist regional and subregional organizations and initiatives, in particular those of the Group of Five for the Sahel (G-5 Sahel). Supporting the G-5 Sahel means providing its Joint Force with the predictable and sustainable logistical and financial support it needs from the United Nations, as well as responding to the essential issues of development and combating climate change that the region faces. The Security Council must be able to anticipate, prevent and seek solutions to counter the effects of climate change, in particular for the most vulnerable populations. The Council’s unity and spirit of compromise are essential in the face of such a challenge. Climate change is a major test for multilateralism. Only coordinated action by all actors, in particular the United Nations, can lead us in the right direction. The Council must therefore be able to better assess and address the impact of climate change on international peace and security and to draw all the necessary conclusions, region by region and subject by subject, for the issues on its agenda. To do that, we cannot rely solely on the commitment of the armed forces and peacekeepers deployed in the peacekeeping operations. In that regard, I would like to commend once again their commitment and sacrifice. To build long-term responses, we also need a way to better understand how climate change and crises are linked and how they reinforce each other so that we may strengthen the resilience of States and their populations. Lastly, as the twenty-sixth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ended a few days ago in Glasgow, we must remember that the cost of inaction would be immense for any of us. That is why France calls on each State to make firm and lasting commitments to reduce

greenhouse-gas emissions in line with the challenges facing our planet. The international community can count on France’s full and complete commitment in that regard.

record.title: Aggression against Ukraine — March 2022
record.proposal_summary: The draft condemns the aggression against Ukraine and demands that Russia end its use of force and withdraw its forces.
record.statement_summary: China said the resolution lacked sufficient consultation and attention to security concerns and diplomatic settlement; it abstained. It also affirmed respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity.
record.setting: The General Assembly's eleventh emergency special session considered a draft on Russia's use of force against Ukraine after the Security Council referred the issue to the Assembly under the Uniting for Peace procedure.

Urges political dialogue, negotiation and mediation to resolve the conflict peacefully.

prompt.content: You are a retrospective policy-memo writer. The upstream content plan supplies the positions, conditions and uncertainty. Express it faithfully as prose. Preserve country, institutional capacity and date. Do not invent facts, agreement, recorded votes or commitments. Distinguish documented positions from analyst proposals. Return only the requested public memo.

SCENARIO
Compare the four delegations' documented positions in the 9 December 2021 climate/security debate. This authored workshop did not occur historically.

Write a policy-analysis memo covering France, the UK, India and Brazil: what is documented common ground, what material differences or conditions remain, and what next steps could be proposed without inventing agreement? Address the questions in each country's brief.
Use at most 700 words, including quoted evidence. Distinguish documented common ground, unresolved differences, and your own proposed next steps. A proposal is not a government commitment. Do not assert that a negotiation or vote occurred.
National questions:
FRA: Based on France’s statement of 9 December 2021, what role should the Security Council play in addressing climate-related insecurity? Explain why a response limited to armed forces and peacekeepers would be insufficient, and identify one complementary measure France supported.
GBR: Summarize the UK’s position on climate-security reporting and participation on 9 December 2021, including what it said about the draft before the Council. Does this statement also establish that the UK had approved binding national carbon quotas imposed by the Council?
IND: An analyst writes: “India objected to a Security Council climate role because it denied that climate change could exacerbate conflict.” Assess this characterization against India’s 9 December 2021 statement. Explain its institutional preference and the qualification in its position.
BRA: What institutional response to climate change did Brazil prefer in its 9 December 2021 statement, and why? Include both its view of climate-related harms and its proposed practical priority.

CONTENT PLAN PROVIDED BY THE UPSTREAM PLANNER
The intended positions and uncertainty are GIVEN. Write a complete prose memo from this plan.
Preserve every national point and its scope. Use the supplied common ground, differences and proposal.
Do not add positions, votes or commitments. References identify the sources behind the plan.

FRA: national UN Security Council delegation; 2021-12-09; S/PV.8923; [climate-fra]
- France supports the Council anticipating, assessing, preventing and addressing climate-related insecurity, particularly for vulnerable populations. [climate-fra]
- Armed forces and peacekeepers alone are insufficient. Longer-term responses need understanding of climate-crisis links and stronger resilience of States and their populations. [climate-fra]
- Complementary measures include better natural-resource allocation and the Great Green Wall. France also supports predictable, sustainable UN logistical and financial support for the G-5 Sahel Joint Force. [climate-fra]

GBR: national UN Security Council delegation; 2021-12-09; S/PV.8923; [climate-gbr]
- The UK supports comprehensive UN reporting on climate-security links, a role for the Security Council alongside other UN bodies, and the submitted draft as an important first step. [climate-gbr]
- The UK supports meaningful participation of women and girls in a fully inclusive approach; their role is not limited to being victims. [climate-gbr]
- This statement does not establish UK approval of Council-imposed binding national carbon quotas. This is an absence of established approval, not evidence of rejection. [climate-gbr]

IND: national UN Security Council delegation; 2021-12-09; S/PV.8923; [climate-ind]
- India acknowledges that climate change has affected lives and exacerbated conflicts. The analyst's claim that India denied every climate-conflict connection is incorrect. [climate-ind]
- India prefers the UNFCCC/COP's inclusive, consensus-driven process with developing-country participation and opposes an alternative Council climate platform that could disrupt that process. [climate-ind]
- India warns against climate-only explanations of conflict and says the effect of climate variability on violence is contested. Attribute this argument to India rather than declaring a settled scientific conclusion. [climate-ind]
- India supports adequate sustainable resources, training and logistics for the G-5 Sahel Joint Force. [climate-ind]

BRA: national UN Security Council delegation; 2021-12-09; S/PV.8923; [climate-bra]
- Brazil prefers the inclusive UNFCCC forum, respecting mandates and avoiding duplication. It objects to reallocating the climate agenda to the Council and cautions against a strict security lens. [climate-bra]
- Brazil acknowledges climate-related threats to health, food and water security and development; Sahel resource depletion can exacerbate tensions and displacement. [climate-bra]
- Brazil prioritizes mobilization, scaling-up and timely delivery of developed-country finance for developing countries, supporting existing commitments and enhanced climate action. [climate-bra]

COMMON GROUND
- All four acknowledge climate-related harms; their descriptions of security links and institutional responses differ. This does not establish all-four endorsement of an existential security threat or a separate Council platform.

DIFFERENCES
- France and the UK support a Council role; India and Brazil prefer climate matters within the inclusive UNFCCC process. Do not attribute a UNFCCC-primary-forum position to all four.
- Explicit G-5 Joint Force support is established for France and India. It is not established by the supplied UK/Brazil statements; that silence does not establish opposition.

PROPOSALS
- Analyst proposal, not an agreed commitment: explore mandate-respecting reporting that preserves the institutional disagreement, and examine timely finance for existing climate commitments without claiming all four endorsed that financing priority.

completion.content:
Comparative policy memo: 9 December 2021 climate/security statements (S/PV.8923)

Documented national positions

France's national Security Council delegation supports anticipating, assessing, preventing and addressing climate-related insecurity, particularly for vulnerable populations. Armed forces and peacekeepers alone are insufficient: longer-term responses require understanding climate-crisis links and strengthening the resilience of States and their populations. Complementary measures include better natural-resource allocation and the Great Green Wall. France supports predictable, sustainable UN logistical and financial support for the G-5 Sahel Joint Force.

The UK supports comprehensive UN reporting on climate-security links and a Council role alongside other UN bodies. It describes the submitted draft as an important first step. Women and girls must participate meaningfully in a fully inclusive approach, beyond being treated as victims. The statement does not establish UK approval of Council-imposed binding national carbon quotas; absence of established approval is not evidence of rejection.

India acknowledges that climate change has affected lives and exacerbated conflicts, so the analyst's absolute-denial characterization is incorrect. India prefers the inclusive, consensus-driven UNFCCC/COP process with developing-country participation and opposes an alternative Council climate platform that could disrupt it. India warns against climate-only explanations of conflict and describes the effect of climate variability on violence as contested. This is India's argument, not a declaration of settled scientific fact. India also supports adequate sustainable resources, training and logistics for the G-5 Sahel Joint Force.

Brazil prefers the inclusive UNFCCC forum, respecting mandates and avoiding duplication. It objects to reallocating the climate agenda to the Council and cautions against a strict security lens. Brazil nevertheless acknowledges climate-related threats to health, food and water security and development; Sahel resource depletion can exacerbate tensions and displacement. Its practical priority is mobilizing, scaling up and delivering developed-country finance for developing countries in a timely way, supporting existing commitments and enhanced climate action.

Documented common ground

All four acknowledge climate-related harms. Their descriptions of security links and institutional responses differ; this does not establish agreement on an existential security threat or a separate Council platform.

Unresolved differences

France and the UK support a Council role; India and Brazil prefer climate matters within the inclusive UNFCCC process. A UNFCCC-primary-forum position is not established for all four. Explicit G-5 Joint Force support is established for France and India, but not by the supplied UK or Brazilian statements. Their silence does not establish opposition.

Proposed next steps

An analyst could explore mandate-respecting reporting that preserves the Council/UNFCCC disagreement and examine timely finance for existing climate commitments. These are proposals, not government commitments or an agreed all-four financing priority. This authored workshop did not historically occur; no negotiation or vote is asserted.

policy_examples.question: A proposed development agreement requires the recipient to change its domestic political system. How does that compare with the white paper's stated approach, and can we infer that every Chinese project complies?
policy_examples.answer: That requirement conflicts with the white paper's stated opposition to political strings and interference in a recipient's chosen development path. It also emphasizes recipient leadership of projects. These are published principles; they do not establish the terms or conduct of every Chinese-financed project. [CHN-development-conditions-2021; CHN-development-recipient-leadership-2021]
